newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Top Russian oil refinery needs cash, quick.
newsitem.headline: Top Russian oil refinery needs cash, quick.

text.p: Russia's massive Kirishi oil refinery, built near St. Petersburg three decades ago, is looking west for investments that are vital to its future.
The plant, known as KINEF, is a rare jewel in the rusting crown of Russian oil refining.
It is coveted above all for its strategic location close to the northwest European oil hub of Rotterdam and for high processing rates -- twin advantages enjoyed by none of Russia's 30 refineries.

But even KINEF is finding it hard to keep its head above water. It will be losing money within three to four years if it fails to garner major loans from foreign banks and companies, financial director Nikolai Laptev said.
"In four years' time, this plant would not be making any money and things would be very difficult without major investment," he said.

In a display of commercial savvy rare for the Soviet Union, the Kremlin in the 1960s chose a site close to the major export outlets of St. Petersburg and the big Baltic ports to build a major new refinery.
Since its completion in 1965, KINEF has come to rely heavily on hard-currency markets in Europe, exporting around 70 percent of its output by 1996.
Many of KINEF's biggest domestic rivals lie thousands of miles from Russia's western border and face huge transit costs to get their products to the Black and Baltic seas by pipeline or railway.

KINEF even looks like a successful business. Trees line the entrance, the directors' offices are modern and clean and the plant's maze of pipelines and units show little of the decay plaguing most of Russia's industrial behemoths.
Another big advantage KINEF has over many competitors is that it already operates well above the industry's average rate.
Laptev said the plant planned to process 16.2 million tons (324,000 barrels per day) of crude oil in 1997, or 98 percent of its annual rated capacity of 16.5 million (330,000 bpd).
The final figure would depend on product prices in the West, since the refinery exports the bulk of its output, he said.
Most Russian refineries, which in total are capable of refining 6.8 million bpd, operate at only 50-60 percent of capacity.
But KINEF has been known to operate beyond its capacity.
"I know that in Soviet times, this plant processed up to 23 million tons (460,000 bpd), but the whole place was shaking in order to do so," said one company official.
Despite all the advantages KINEF enjoys, the plant sees no future without hundreds of millions of dollars of foreign investment.

The key to its survival lies in building a new and costly hydrocracking unit, which would enable it to produce more expensive oil products such as gasoline and jet fuel and reduce its dependence on lower-value products like heavy fuel oil.

Moving from the heavier end of the barrel to the lighter end is an aim common to all of Russia's biggest refineries -- but not one has yet succeeded in getting a major upgrade funded by foreign investment off the ground.
Given that a hydrocracker takes four years to install, time is not on KINEF's side. And financing the facility is not likely to be easy, considering the huge sums involved.
The cost of the hydrocracker initially weighs in at $750 million, but after loan servicing, the bill nearly doubles.
"If you include all additional costs -- taxes and others -- the cost would be in the realm of $1.3 billion," Laptev said.

Talks between the refinery and Western companies and banks on raising cash have already begun, but they are still in a preliminary stage. Laptev declined to give details on which companies were involved and what form any investment would take. Vladimir Bogdanov, president of Surgutneftegaz, said the company was working with German and U.S. organisations.
KINEF has already gone some way toward attracting foreign investment and has two small projects with European partners.

The plant began producing world-class jet fuel for the first time in February, which it sells to international airlines flying in and out of St. Petersburg. But the identity of the Western firm involved remains hush-hush.

KINEF also produces special products used in the manufacture of detergents in a venture with Yugoslav partners. The facility produces 50,000 tons of products a year, with Procter & Gamble Co. among its customers.
